🟡 Bioregional Weaving Alliance Ireland

Bioregional Organizer
🌐 Visit website

BWL South East Ireland is a bioregional initiative functioning as a transition hub, learning centre, and living lab. It brings together a network of Irish stakeholders, partners, and the living systems of the region itself. Established as a non-profit in 2022 and formally constituted in 2024.

Bioregional Context

The bioregion is centered around the Bride Valley in Ireland and includes the village of Dunhill, which is part of the Copper Coast UNESCO Geopark. The landscape is primarily agricultural, with a mix of dairy farms, grazing lands, and areas being transformed for nature conservation.

Background

The Bride Valley, which is part of the Copper Coast UNESCO Geopark, is characterized by a primarily agricultural landscape—a mix of dairy farms, grazing lands, and areas being transformed for nature conservation. Multiple generations of family farms form the backbone of the local economy, creating a context where sustainable transitions must work with existing farming communities rather than replacing them.

Origins and Network

The Bioregional Weaving Alliance Ireland (BWA Ireland) is a bioregional initiative functioning as a transition hub, learning centre, and living lab. Established as a non-profit in 2022, the organization brings together a network of Irish stakeholders, partners, and the living systems of the region itself.

The organization is involved in a 'deep demonstration' partnership with the Irish government to test landscape approaches to the future of sustainable dairy, positioning them to establish the Bioregional Weaving Alliance as an entity designed to support learning and initiatives leading to bioregional regeneration, restoration, and protection, especially in the South East.

Activities

🔸

Family Land Biodiversity Index

A project involving 43 farmers with the goal of ensuring at least 10% of farmland is dedicated to biodiversity while maintaining farm viability. To this end, they developed the Family Land Biodiversity Index (FBI), a tool designed to reward farmers for ecological stewardship. Unlike traditional conservation schemes that rely on static subsidies for setting aside land, the FBI is a results-based incentive system with four components: biodiversity survey, farm-specific biodiversity plans, annual biodiversity scoring, and results-based payments. The project developed a digital tools to accurately measure space for nature on farms and verify the ecological quality of these areas. The outcomes of the project were exciting. Farmers reported 5–10% revenue increases through diversified income sources, such as agroforestry and eco-tourism. The 43-farm discussion group created a strong social fabric, and even neighboring farms started creating their own habitat corridors. This created biodiversity gains including pollinator population recovery, recovery of ground-nesting bird species, and improved soil health. The FBI model is now being considered for wider agricultural policy reforms at the national and EU level.

🔸

Sustainable Dairy Index

Building on the FBI system, the team developed the Sustainable Dairy Index, a systematic effort to redefine success metrics in dairy farming by integrating environmental and social returns alongside financial ones. The program introduces frameworks for measuring social contributions, recognizing that when farmers depend on other farmers, they create circular economies and sustainable economies.

🔸

Dunhill Ecopark Development Initiative

Dunhill Ecopark is a community-scale hub meant to combine living, working, learning, and enterprise: roughly 38 businesses already operate on-site, with education spaces anchoring how people encounter regenerative agriculture and reflect on environmental, social, and economic impacts together. A planned on-site milk-processing facility would keep more value from regenerative dairy in the territory—linking premium products to fair returns for farmers. The hub mixes earned income, grants, and investment so the site can stay viable while the model is tested at scale.

🔸

Regenerative Agriculture Demonstration Network

Demonstration farms knit neighboring holdings into a learning network—sharing practices and materials in place. One early experiment uses waste wool as mulch around aronia berries. The longer-term bet is that these sites become reference points: for farmers trying new crops, for visitors relearning relationships to food and land, and for shifts in what people grow, buy, and expect from the landscape.

🔸

Waterford Bioregional Mapping

Mapping work combines science and lived attachment. Participatory workshops ask residents where they feel emotionally tied to the territory; those insights layer onto geological base maps of river basins and land use. In the Anne Valley, community-led water-quality monitoring adds ground-truth to institutional data. Throughout, the process engages Gaeltacht na nDéise (Irish-speaking Waterford) so language and culture stay visible in how the bioregion is drawn and discussed.

Vision and Legacy

Through their deep demonstration partnership with the Irish government and their portfolio of initiatives, BWA Ireland is positioned to serve as a vessel for change—inspiring farmers, communities, and visitors to participate in regenerative practices that benefit nature, farmers, economy, and inspiration. The work demonstrates how locally-driven initiatives can scale up through policy influence (as with the FBI model), while maintaining strong community roots and collaboration at the bioregional level.
